subject: biology
title: Evolution & Biodiversity Adventure 3: Hardy-Weinberg and speciation
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and watch species split.
meta_desc: IBDP Biology — Hardy-Weinberg p²+2pq+q², allopatric and sympatric speciation, polyploidy.
final_note: You learned p²+2pq+q²=1 predicts allele frequencies, allopatric speciation needs geographic barriers, and sympatric speciation can occur via polyploidy.

walkthroughs.body_html:
For a gene with two alleles (A frequency p, a frequency q):

p + q = 1
p² + 2pq + q² = 1

Equilibrium needs no mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, large population. Deviations from H-W reveal evolution acting.

In a population, 16% show recessive phenotype (q² = 0.16).

q = 0.4, so p = 0.6.
Heterozygotes 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48 (48%).
Homozygous dominant p² = 0.36 (36%).

So even with 60% dominant allele, only 36% are AA.

Allopatric — geographic barrier (mountain rise, river change) splits population. Each evolves independently → reproductive isolation. Galápagos finches.

Sympatric — same area; usually via polyploidy (whole-genome duplication). Common in plants — wheat is hexaploid (6n). New polyploid cannot breed with original → instant species.

mcqs.q: Polyploidy commonly drives which speciation type?

numericals.q: In a population, 9% of individuals are homozygous recessive. What percentage are heterozygous? (q²=0.09)

free_texts.q: What word describes whole-genome duplication, often producing new plant species? One word.
